article_content: Tens of thousands of Ethiopians gathered for a state funeral honoring Tilahun Gessesse, a singer often censored by the government for his politically charged lyrics. Despite his legacy, Tilahun was exiled during the Derg regime but later pardoned. His songs, though sometimes critical of authority, were embraced by all regimes. Mourners filled the streets, and security struggled to control crowds as the nation bid farewell to a man many call 'the father of Ethiopian music.' Radio stations interrupted programming for his memorial. Hours before, fans gathered in Addis Ababa's main square under the scorching sun, chanting and singing his songs. Antene Gizachew, 50, said no one can replace him in Ethiopia's heart. 'He's a legend for Africa,' Gizachew said. 'He was a motivator, humanitarian, like our Elvis. He lives forever in Ethiopians' hearts.' Tilahun's voice united a struggling nation, transcending politics and time. He was a favorite of Emperor Haile Selassie and served in the Imperial Guards. His fame grew under the Derg regime when he was briefly exiled for his music. He traveled abroad, raising millions for famine victims during the 'We Are the World' campaign. Unlike others who fled the Derg, he returned and entertained troops during the Eritrean war, earning the current government's respect. Government officials attended his service, along with a bouquet from Teddy Afro, sentenced for a fatal accident. Artist Sileshi Demisse noted Tilahun's music sometimes had a political edge, but he wasn't anti-government. 'He expressed feelings during all regimes,' Demisse said. Actor Abdullah Balcha, Tilahun's attorney, said he expressed the people's feelings in multiple languages. Tilahun struggled with diabetes and died at 68 after returning from the U.S.

article_content: PENTAGON - The U.S. military service chiefs have sought an indefinite delay before allowing transgender people to enlist, citing major setbacks in integration. A final decision has been made to repeal the policy, according to Pentagon chief spokesperson Dana White. Transgender troops already in the military have been allowed to serve openly since July 2016, but this policy is now under review. The U.S. armed forces were given until July 1 to develop policies to let transgender individuals who meet all the standards to join the military, but this deadline has been widely criticized as unrealistic. The Associated Press reported earlier Friday that the chiefs were seeking a six-month delay, but sources indicate the pause could be much longer. Deputy Secretary of Defense Robert Work has received recommendations from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps and is having further conversations before submitting his own recommendation to Defense Secretary Jim Mattis. 'Different services had different takes,' White said. 'Some asked for time.' The recommendation will be made with a focus on how the U.S. military can best achieve lethality and readiness. Should the deputy secretary approve the delay, Mattis will need to make a final decision. It is unclear whether that will happen before the July 1 deadline, but sources suggest the delay is likely to be extended.

article_content: 25.10.2023 Russian Defence Minister General of the Army Sergei Shoigu inspected the advanced command post of the Donetsk Liberation Front in the South Donetsk direction during a working visit to the special military operation zone. At the command post, the head of the Russian Defence Ministry received reports from the Group Commander and HQ officers on the current situation, the nature of the enemy's actions, and the fulfilment by the Russian troops of combat tasks in the main tactical areas. Commander of the Donetsk Liberation Front Lieutenant General Andrey Kuzmenko reported on the implementation of the Russian Defence Minister's instructions to create regular UAV units within subordinate troops, staff them with qualified specialists, and equip all units with unmanned aerial systems for strike and reconnaissance, including FPV drones. In addition, the Group's Commander reported to the head of the military department on the specifics of the tactics used by the Group's assault detachments in cooperation with reconnaissance and fire systems in combat missions to seize terrorist strongholds by assault groups. During the meeting at the Group's command post, the Minister of Defence of the Russian Federation received reports from the chiefs of arms and services on issues relating to the organisation of counter-battery warfare. The Russian Minister of Defence heard separate reports from the heads of the relevant services on the readiness of the Group for winter operations, as well as the availability of heating stoves and methods for keeping military personnel warm. Sergei Shoigu brought to the notice of the Commander and leaders the importance of promptly and adequately supplying all Group personnel with new winter clothes and creating an on-hand reserve of insulated footwear and winter uniforms. It was also noted that the supply of winter clothes was supported by international humanitarian organizations. Department for Media Affairs and Information

article_content: Fourteen states and one U.S. territory are set to host a critical series of primaries next week, an event that could dramatically shift the balance of power in the Democratic race. With over a third of the delegates at stake, this Super Tuesday has the potential to make or break campaigns. A candidate needs 1,991 delegates to secure the Democratic nomination, and next week's contests will allocate a significant portion of them. The early states have already shown a strong preference for progressive candidates, signaling a shift in the party's direction. Bernie Sanders, fresh from decisive victories in New Hampshire and Nevada, is poised to solidify his position as the clear front-runner. His message of democratic socialism is resonating widely, especially among younger voters. Michael Bloomberg, despite his late entry into the race, is emerging as a formidable contender. His unprecedented spending on campaign ads has allowed him to gain traction in states like Texas, where he is challenging Sanders directly. The contests in California and Texas will be particularly consequential, with 415 and 228 delegates up for grabs, respectively. These states will play a crucial role in determining the momentum of the race moving forward. Smaller states like Oklahoma and Arkansas also have the opportunity to influence the outcome, as their delegates could swing the balance in favor of moderate candidates like Joe Biden or Pete Buttigieg. The Democratic Party's threshold of 15% for delegate allocation could exclude several candidates from earning delegates, potentially narrowing the field significantly after Super Tuesday. Results are expected to be available shortly after polls close, but the complexity of California's vote-counting process could delay final results for several days or even weeks.
